input.question: How is it possible that socalled "red meat" affects our body more then fish and chicken?
input.ground_truth: Red meats have a much higher concentration of myoglobin, a protein that makes red meats look "redder." Myoglobin is similar to hemoglobin, the protein that makes your blood red and both proteins also contain iron. Myoglobin and hemoglobin are used to store oxygen, one of the vital compounds needed for our body to produce energy. The issue with cancer is that myoglobin is broken down during digestion but not fully absorbed. Much of the iron and other broken protein parts will end up going through your large intestines (colon). These products stimulate the cells in your colon to grow which can lead to cancerous growths.

Question: How is it possible that socalled "red meat" affects our body more then fish and chicken?

response.prediction:
Okay, let's imagine your body is like a playground.

When you eat different foods, they give your body different kinds of "building blocks" and "energy."

"Red meat" is like bringing a big, heavy box of building blocks to the playground. These blocks are a little different from the ones you get from fish or chicken. Some of these blocks, called "iron" and "fat," are found in bigger amounts in red meat. Sometimes, too many of these blocks (like a lot of iron or a certain kind of fat) can make your body feel different, like giving you more energy but sometimes making you feel heavy or not so healthy if you eat too much.

Fish and chicken are like bringing smaller, lighter boxes. They also have building blocks, but not as much of those special ones that can make a big difference. Fish even has something called "omega-3," which is like a super helpful block that helps your brain and heart stay happy and healthy.

So, red meat can change your body a bit more because it has more of certain building blocks, but that doesn’t always mean it’s bad—it just means it can have a bigger effect, either good or not-so-good, depending on how much you eat and how often.
